title: Policy evaluation engine — constraints, scoring, explainability logs (draft)
content:
Purpose
-----
These are working notes for the policy evaluation engine that sits in the control plane and decides per-request routing and fallback behavior. Focus areas: constraint checking, scoring/utility functions, and the explainability log schema we will emit for auditing and offline diagnostics. This doc is intentionally pragmatic — contains pseudocode and open questions. Goal is to converge on an implementation that fits the multi-region, multi-tier routing model used by Redwood: hosted, dedicated, private.

Context and scope
-----------------
Where this lives: control plane service (policy-eval), called synchronously on request admit (hot path) with a small/fast cache for frequently used keys. The runtime (serving nodes) must be able to independently apply a subset of rules when control-plane unavailable (graceful degradation).

Primary responsibilities
- Enforce hard constraints (tenant entitlements, region affinity, compliance tags, model compatibility).
- Compute soft scores (latency cost, unit-cost estimate, model-quality score, load-sensitivity) to rank candidate routes.
- Emit explainability logs summarizing decision factors used for routing.
- Provide deterministic tie-breaking and versioned policies for reproducibility.

Design principles
-----------------
- Minimal p95 evaluation time (target 2ms median, 10ms p99 for cache hits).
- Deterministic outcomes for same inputs + policy version.
- Human-readable explain logs with structured fields for offline analysis.
- Fail-safe defaults: if evaluation fails, prefer the most conservative route (region fallback + trusted model).
- Small trust boundary: control plane returns signed decisions with a short TTL so edge/runtime can validate.

High-level flow (synchronous call)
---------------------------------
1) Request arrives at front proxy with metadata: tenant_id, route, model_hint, origin_region, SLA_hint, request_tags (PII, regulated, latency_profile).
2) Proxy queries policy-eval with these inputs + cached token.
3) policy-eval expands tenant policy, global defaults, and active constraints for that tenant.
4) Filter candidate backends (region+pool+model) via hard constraints.
5) Score remaining candidates with weighted utility function.
6) Apply tie-breaker deterministic rule and produce final route + alternative fallback list.
7) Return signed decision and explainability log to proxy.
8) Proxy logs the explain log and routes request.

Constraint model
----------------
- Types: hard, soft. Hard constraints are boolean filters (deny). Soft constraints only influence scoring.
- Examples of hard constraints: model not approved for tenant, tenant requires dedicated-only, region block due to legal restriction, KMS/HSM unavailable, data sovereignty flags.
- Examples of soft constraints: preferred region, cost sensitivity tag, preferred GPU type, recent QPS load.
- Policy representation: ordered list of named constraints with short-circuit evaluation for hard denies. Each constraint has a version id and applied_scope (global, tenant, team).

Constraint evaluation pseudocode
-------------------------------
// Inputs: request, candidateBackends, policyVersion
function filterHardConstraints(request, candidateBackends, policy) {
  allowed = []
  for backend in candidateBackends: 
    allowedBackend = true
    for c in policy.hardConstraints: 
      if not evaluateConstraint(c, request, backend):
        allowedBackend = false
        break // short-circuit on first deny
    if allowedBackend: allowed.append(backend)
  return allowed
}

Scoring and utility function
---------------------------
We use a linear combination of normalized factors to compute a composite score (higher is better). Factors are normalized to [0,1]. We store weights per-tenant (defaults at global).
Score(backend) = w_quality*Q + w_latency*(1 - normLatency) + w_cost*(1 - normCost) + w_load*(1 - normLoad) + w_affinity*affinityScore
Where: Q is model-quality estimate (0..1), normLatency is historical p95 normalized against SLA target, normCost normalized expected token cost, normLoad normalized current pool utilization, affinityScore is 1.0 if region/pool matches tenant preference otherwise a fractional value.

Notes on components:
- Model-quality (Q): derived from eval runs on tenant workload samples (periodic). If missing, default to model family baseline.
- Latency: combine regional network latency and backend p95; prefer backends that meet SLA headroom.
- Cost: estimate tokens * per-token unit cost for backend model variant. Cache token-estimates for typical prompts.
- Load: use recent utilization metrics (10s window) with exponential smoothing.

Scoring pseudocode
------------------
function scoreBackends(backends, weights, metricsStore, tenantProfiles) {
  results = []
  for b in backends: 
    Q = tenantProfiles.getModelQuality(b.model, b.version) or globalBaseline(b.model)
    latency = metricsStore.getP95(b)
    cost = priceCatalog.estimate(b.model, b.quantization)
    load = metricsStore.getLoad(b.pool)
    affinity = computeAffinity(b, request)
    score = weights.w_quality*Q + weights.w_latency*(1 - normalize(latency)) + weights.w_cost*(1 - normalize(cost)) + weights.w_load*(1 - normalize(load)) + weights.w_affinity*affinity
    results.append({
      "backend": b.id,
      "score": score,
      "components": ["Q="+str(Q), "latency="+str(latency), "cost="+str(cost), "load="+str(load), "affinity="+str(affinity)]
    })
  return sortByScoreDesc(results)
}

Explainability logs (schema)
---------------------------
We will emit a compact JSON-serializable explain record per request. Key goals: auditability, reproducibility, compactness for 90-day ingest into observability. Use short field names to keep size small when logged frequently.
Proposed fields (flat):
- ts: ISO timestamp
- req_id: request UUID
- tenant: tenant_id
- policy_version: string
- input_summary: comma-separated short tags (e.g., "pii,high_latency_sla")
- candidates: pipe-separated backend ids that passed hard constraints ("r-us-1:gpuA|r-eu-1:cpuB")
- chosen: backend id chosen
- score_components: semicolon-separated key=value pairs ("Q=0.92;latency=0.12;cost=0.03;load=0.45;aff=1")
- decision_reason: short code (e.g., "SCORE_MAX", "HARD_FALLBACK", "CONTROL_PLANE_ERROR")
- signed_ttl: seconds until decision signature expires
- policy_hash: sha1 of policy blob used (to link to stored policy in DB)
- trace_id: optional trace link for distributed tracing
- debug_notes: short text when debug flag set (avoid in prod logs unless sampled)

Example record (compact):
{
  "ts":"2026-02-19T18:23:12Z",
  "req_id":"r_0a1b2c3d",
  "tenant":"acme-corp",
  "policy_version":"v2026-02-15-5",
  "input_summary":"pii,low_latency",
  "candidates":"us-west-1:gA|us-east-1:gB",
  "chosen":"us-west-1:gA",
  "score_components":"Q=0.87;latency=0.08;cost=0.12;load=0.21;aff=1",
  "decision_reason":"SCORE_MAX",
  "signed_ttl":"30",
  "policy_hash":"sha1:abcdef123456...",
  "trace_id":"01-abc-trace-xyz",
  "debug_notes":"none"
}

Explain log retention and privacy
--------------------------------
- Retain explain logs 90 days by default. For high-sensitivity tenants (PII), retain only aggregated metrics unless the tenant has opted into detailed logs and accepted compliance requirements.
- Mask tenant-identifying fields in logs for shared analytics (hash tenant id).
- Access to raw explain logs strictly role-based; separate pipeline for compliance/forensics with audit.

Versioning and determinism
-------------------------
- Every policy change creates a new policy_version. policy_hash included in explain log for reproducibility.
- Deterministic sort for tie-breaks: lexicographic backend id + policy_version seed.
- Randomized sampling only used for non-critical A/B experiments and must be logged with seed.

Multi-region concerns
---------------------
Propagation model:
- Policies are authored in control plane and asynchronously pushed to region control-plane replicas. Synchronous evaluation uses the global control-plane unless a region-local evaluation is configured (private deployments).
- To reduce latency we allow region-local cached policy replicas with TTL and last-modified vector clock. Each decision emitted includes policy_version and policy_hash so decisions can be audited after the fact.
- For cross-region requests (origin != data-region) enforce hard constraints early for data sovereignty.

Consistency tradeoffs:
- Strong consistency (global read of policy) increases p99 and dependency on control-plane availability.
- Eventual consistency (local cached policy) reduces latency at cost of slightly stale policy behavior. We prefer eventual with short TTLs and strong auditability (policy_hash).

Rollback and safe deploys
------------------------
- Canary: enable new policy for X% of tenant traffic and sample explain logs for manual review.
- Shadow testing: run new policy in shadow to compare decisions without affecting routing. Record divergence metrics.
- Auto-rollback: if divergence in critical constraints or if p99 eval time spikes beyond threshold, revert local policy to previous version.

Runtime considerations and perf
----------------------------
- Cache hot evaluations keyed by (tenant_id, route, model_hint, policy_version) with small LRU and TTL 30s. Cache stores signed decision to allow runtime verification.
- Metrics to collect: eval_latency histogram, cache_hit_rate, avg_candidates_after_filter, top_decision_reasons, divergence_rate during canary.
- C++ core for hot path with thin Go wrapper for policy authoring + storage? We should prototype in Go and extract hot loop into Rust/C++ later.

Security and signatures
----------------------
- Decisions are signed with short-lived asymmetric key pair. Runtime validates signature to avoid trusting malformed decisions from compromised control plane instance.
- Key rotation handled by central KMS; old keys stay valid to verify recent decisions for TTL window.

Open questions / tradeoffs (needs input)
-------------------------------------
1) How much of scoring weights should be tenant-editable vs. admin-only? (security surface)
2) Should model-quality (Q) be tenant-specific baseline (better personalization) or globally smoothed to prevent gaming?
3) Explain log size: do we compress or sample heavy-valued fields? Storage cost vs. interpretability.
4) Policy authoring UX: DSL vs. JSON blobs vs. GUI. DSL increases complexity but reduces accidental misconfig.
5) Rollout threshold for canary — default 5%? 1%?

Implementation plan (next 6 weeks)
---------------------------------
Week 0-1: finalize schema for policy and explain log, select tech stack (Go + small Rust scoring lib). (Owner: Diego)
Week 2: implement hard-constraint filter and signed decision proto; basic unit tests. (Owner: Lin)
Week 3-4: implement scoring engine + weights, metrics instrumentation + basic integration test with front proxy. (Owner: Priya)
Week 5: build canary/shadow harness + divergence metrics and smoke multi-region replica behavior. Deploy to staging. (Owner: Aisha)
Week 6: collect feedback, address perf outliers, finalize docs and RFC for platform review.

Tickets and reference artifacts
------------------------------
- PLAT-834 : policy-eval initial implementation (tracking ticket)
- GH PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/789 (prototype branch)
- Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/PLAT/Policy+Evaluation+Overview

Appendix: small example scenarios
--------------------------------
1) Tenant requires dedicated-only and model family X banned for that tenant. Filter will remove all shared pool backends and any backend with model family X. Explain log will include decision_reason=HARD_FILTER and candidates empty -> fallback flow to support team.
2) Two backends match; backend A has slightly worse cost but much better Q. With weights w_quality=0.6, w_cost=0.2, w_latency=0.1, w_load=0.1 downstream picks A. Explain log shows score_components Q dominates.

Next steps (for reviewers)
-------------------------
- Please review scoring formula assumptions and list any missing factors (e.g., energy/carbonscore?).
- Comment on privacy handling for explain logs (do we need tenant opt-in flow?).
- Confirm canary percentage defaults and rollback thresholds.

Quick links:
- RFC draft PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/789
- Tracking ticket: PLAT-834

Notes to self:
- Keep the explain log compact; consider adding a numeric codebook for common decision_reasons to save bytes.
- If latency requirements tighten, consider moving constraint filtering to edge for certain non-sensitive checks.

---
End of draft.
